### [Gandalf: Flash Shall Not Die! Increasing Flash Storage Lifetime for KV Cache Offloading in LLM Serving](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30791>)

Gandalf manages offloaded attention caches across host memory and solid-state drives, using attention type, expected reuse and write wear to decide which states to retain, move or recompute. Its trace-based evaluation shows how avoiding low-value writes can extend projected drive endurance, giving serving-system designers an explicit way to trade cache misses against storage wear rather than optimizing hit rate alone.

**Published:** 2026-10-22 · **First seen:** 2026-10-23T10:06:01.348Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** KV Offloading, SSD Endurance, Tiered Storage, Hybrid Attention

**Public availability:** 2026-10-23T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30791v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Full14-page pinned v1 PDF and HTML methods/results inspected. The central contribution is a storage admission/placement policy, category3.7. Full-attention prefixes can be reused across successive turns, whereas recurrent/linear states are often reused only at the next turn and then superseded. Each admitted state first enters DRAM; under pressure Gandalf compares a leaf-drop cost with moving a root-side candidate to SSD, counting estimated next-reuse recomputation benefit, object size, idle age, SSD purchase price per rated write byte and the loss from replacing an SSD victim. An optional target-lifetime multiplier prices writes more aggressively when the write budget is overspent. Lazy heaps over prefix-tree leaf/frontier candidates reduce scoring work. The online rule approximates an offline objective; it is not a proved optimal replacement algorithm. Main evaluation uses three traces (Qwen Bailian TraceA, ClaudeCode WEKA SemiAnalysis, and a400K-request/100-turn AIPerf workload), a Kimi-K3 hybrid configuration with72% linear-attention layers,100GB host DRAM and1TB/4TB SSD capacities, and six policies adapted to the same two-tier capacity. At the minimum-miss setting in Section5.2, ClaudeCode has Gandalf miss ratio0.052 versus0.045 for Marconi/0.047 for LRU, while the latter write3.3× more SSD bytes; projected rated-endurance lifetime follows the write-volume reduction. The paper separately models a practical tradeoff at alpha1:17.0 versus4.0 months projected life at0.78 versus0.66seconds modeled cache-load latency, assuming10GB/s SSD,50GB/s host-to-GPU transfer and60Ktokens/s recomputation. This is not measured end-to-end GPU latency. Receipt is2026-10-22T06:10:08Z; the original FridayOct23 cs.LG batch and official Thursday20:00US/Eastern schedule imply announcement2026-10-23T00:00Z. Exact-title screening did not establish an earlier public Gandalf method. No author implementation/project release destination was verified; background LMCache/vLLM links are not presented as Gandalf source code.

**Limitations:** Principal comparative results are trace-based simulation, with small-scale FEMU emulator calibration and an author-stated LMCache/vLLM integration; the paper does not provide measured physical drive wear-out or deployment throughput demonstrating the policy. Lifetime means time to consume rated TBW under indefinitely repeated traces, a1DWPD/five-year rating and write-amplification factor1. SSD garbage collection, internal wear leveling, changing production mixes and physical failure uncertainty are not modeled, so lifetime is a projection and can be optimistic. The headline7.3× average does not describe every matched miss-rate setting; alpha can incur large miss penalties (TraceA0.818 versus LRU0.697 at alpha1), and the paper’s separate analyses use different settings. Cache-load latency assumes transfer/recomputation overlap and fixed rates; it is not whole-request TTFT or a hardware benchmark. Next-turn reuse/type assumptions fit append-only hybrid workloads, not arbitrary cache branching or all architectures. Heap candidate pruning is validated on two traces, not universally lossless. No independent reproduction or verified public Gandalf code release; extension to high-bandwidth flash is future work.

### [Coordination-Free Workload Regularization for Variable-Cost Distributed Training](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21162>)

Batch Cost Lookahead buffers a bounded window inside each training worker and regroups it into equal-record-count batches with similar estimated cost, without exchanging sample metadata across workers. This reduces synchronization waiting for variable-length training while retaining the existing batch-count interface, with explicit diagnostics for oversized records and persistent imbalance that local scheduling cannot fix.

**Published:** 2026-10-15 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:02:23.754Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Data Loading, Load Balancing, Sequence Packing, Distributed Training

**Public availability:** 2026-10-16T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21162>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Editorial catch-up of an October16 arXiv announcement already screened as a reserve on October17; this is delayed selection, not an indexing-delay claim. Read Sections1-10, Algorithm1 and all evaluation tables. The fixed-cardinality contract conserves each window's records and uses classical longest-processing-time initialization plus bounded heavy/light swaps. On Llama3.2-1B NeMo-RL0.7.0 SFT with FSDP2/BF16/FA3 on eight H200 GPUs, lookahead32 versus1 in the same per-rank pipeline improves mean wall-clock step speed by0.4-30.5% across11 corpora, over three300-step repeats excluding20warmups. All arms use the same per-corpus p99 cap. The abstract's5.0-16.7% comparison against pooledMFFD includes input-path differences and is cross-campaign. Paper receipt is October15 03:22:50Z; public availability is inferred from the original cs.DC Friday16 batch and official Thursday20:00Eastern schedule.

**Limitations:** The assignment heuristic is classical; the contribution is its bounded streaming deployment contract and measured boundary analysis, not a new global optimizer. Length-cost simulation is not GPU speedup. Two matched no-lookahead arms were not rerun after prior OOMs. The larger1.197-1.343x result uses an internal sequential recommender and weak scaling from8to32H200 ranks, not LLM scaling evidence. Local reordering cannot resolve a dominant infeasible record or different total cost across rank shards. It changes optimizer-step sample grouping; p99 truncation quality, held-out SFT quality and exact midstream restart are untested. No dedicated public implementation was verified; no independent reproduction.

### [Leto: Fast In-Place Recovery for LLM Training on Surviving Hardware](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00687>)

Leto retains recoverable model state outside a failed training process and prepares a shadow process on the same hardware, using protected memory and transactional updates to resume consistently. For failures that leave accelerators usable, this avoids checkpoint reloads and repeated training work, reducing the time otherwise spent recovering idle GPUs.

**Published:** 2026-09-30 · **First seen:** 2026-10-02T15:33:57Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Fault Tolerance, Training Recovery, Checkpointing

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00687>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Catch-up discovery: v1 was submitted September 30 at 20:29:57 UTC but appears in the October 2 announcement list; the official schedule implies October 2 00:00 UTC public release. On 6- and 72-A100 testbeds, five model workloads recover in 6–19 seconds, reported as 3.6–6.5x faster than their best checkpointing baseline; fault-injection tests also check recovery consistency.

**Limitations:** The fast path requires hardware-operable failures; fatal failures still use checkpoints. Measurements inject failures, and very large cluster claims are simulations. Protection and shadow processes add overhead, including a small regression when all failures are fatal; a public Leto implementation was not verified.

### [6x faster Async Checkpointing in PyTorch, using Cached Plans, no GIL contention](<https://pytorch.org/blog/6x-faster-async-checkpointing/>)

PyTorch distributed checkpointing moves background saving into a separate process and reuses save plans to reduce Python lock contention and expensive metadata collectives. These changes keep checkpoint persistence from depressing training throughput for as long, making frequent recovery checkpoints more affordable at large GPU counts.

**Published:** 2025-04-30 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T04:13:56.564Z · **Novelty:** baseline · **Tags:** Checkpointing, Fault Tolerance, PyTorch

**Positioning:** open-reference

[Blog](<https://pytorch.org/blog/6x-faster-async-checkpointing/>) · [Code](<https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict_saver.py>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. Meta and Crusoe report a Llama-3-70B/TorchTitan run on 1,856 H200 GPUs where background checkpoint processing fell from about 436 to 67 seconds, with GPU-to-CPU staging taking about 0.78 seconds.

**Limitations:** The 6.5x figure concerns background checkpoint processing, not overall model training. Benefit depends on storage, checkpoint structure, and repeated plans; initial planning and coordinator metadata remain costs.
